power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Past research has strongly emphasized the role of dark personality, particularly, the dark triad/tetrad in malevolent creativity.
However, reported associations largely stem from self-report measures (e.g., the Malevolent Creativity Behavior Scale: MCBS), which has received criticism.
For this reason, in two-independent studies, this paper scrutinizes the relevance of the dark triad/tetrad for performance in a malevolent creativity test (MCT).
Associations were tested for total malevolent creativity, and followed up for originality, malevolence, and fluency of ideas.

In study 1 (n = 307), neither correlations nor multiple regression models revealed any significant association of narcissism, Machiavellianism, or psychopathy with malevolent creativity performance metrics.
In study 2 (n = 287), correlations between the dark tetrad and MCT creativity metrics were equally non-significant.
Only in multiple regression models, a combination of high Machiavellianism, high psychopathy, and high sadism (three-way interaction) predicted higher total malevolent creativity.

Overall, associations with MCT creativity metrics did not surpass small effects of f² = 0.02, showing that the apparently robust findings from malevolent creativity self-report do not replicate in malevolent creativity performance tests.
It is thus possible that the dark triad/tetrad may be less relevant for malevolent idea generation that previously assumed.

In recent years, creativity research has experienced a rather prominent surge of investigations into malevolent creativity -creative ideas intentionally generated and/or implemented to harm others (Cropley et al., 2008).

text.text: Research has therefore examined both (a) whether ordinary, yet creative people have harmful capacities (i.e., malevolent creativity in the general population) and (b) whether people who are evidently capable of doing harmful things, are also creative (i.e., malevolent creativity in prisoners, terrorists).

Having obtained a rich repertoire of empirical findings on cognitive, affective, personality, and contextual aspects of malevolent creativity, scholars now devote more attention to building comprehensive frameworks and models of how, when, and why malevolent creative ideas may occur, and under which circumstances they may be implemented, ultimately leading to malevolent innovation (d 'Amato & Hunter, 2025; Kapoor & Kaufman, 2022a; Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025).

text.text: Among individual mechanisms supposedly facilitating malevolent creativity, dark personality traits seem to have received the most attention.

While earlier studies reported positive links of malevolent creativity to aggressiveness and impulsivity (Lee & Dow, 2011; Harris & Reiter-Palmon, 2015), later works have also obtained positive links to trait deception, low morality, or antagonism as a general maladaptive personality domain (Kapoor et al., 2025; Kapoor & Kaufman, 2022b; Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2021a).

text.text: The elements of the dark triad/tetrad include: Narcissism, comprising grandiosity, entitlement, status-seeking, and need for admiration; Machiavellianism, reflecting strategic manipulation, a cynical worldview, and instrumental exploitation; psychopathy, composed of fearlessness, shallow affect, lack of empathy, and impulsivity; and sadism, enjoyment of cruelty and suffering of others (see Paulhus, 2014; Paulhus & Dutton, 2016).

text.text: Rarely, it seems, has research yielded such unequivocal insights, and one may be led to believe (or fear) that individuals higher in dark triad/tetrad traits also wield a dangerous amount of malevolent creativity.
However critically, evidence is mounting that studies linking dark tetrad traits with malevolent creativity may overstate the strength and/or significance of this relationship.
First, findings have been almost exclusively obtained with self-reports of malevolent creativity (like in the MCBS).
Yet, such self-report does not automatically equal a higher capacity for malevolent idea generation, and such inference may be problematic on several accounts.

In general, various studies show that self-perceived creativity, creative performance in psychometric tests (i.e., the cognitive ability to spontaneously generate creative ideas) and creative achievements (i.e., real-life outcomes, e.g., for malevolent creativity, successful creative war strategies) are not necessarily highly correlated, often only showing weak links with each other (see Pretz & McCollum, 2014; Reiter-Palmon et al., 2012; Said-Metwaly et al., 2024).

text.text: Moreover, while the accuracy and validity of creativity self-reports may be questioned in general (for arguments why they are still useful, see Kaufman, 2019), using them to approximate creative performance is a bigger issue when examining those with inflated self-perceptions (narcissism), or strategic exploitation of others (Machiavellianism). Kapoor (2015) notes that narcissists in particular are likely to feign goodness and creativity for personal gain, and often succeed at convincing others of their positive creative abilities (also see Goncalo et al., 2010), though they likely do not have them (see Lebuda et al., 2021).

text.text: Thus, narcissists may underreport malevolent creativity, while individuals higher in Machiavellianism may both under-or overreport, depending on their evaluation on what can be gained from the current context.
For psychopathy, two perspectives are possible.

While Lebuda et al. (2021) suggest that creativity self-reports of people higher in psychopathy may be quite accurate, as they care little about opinions of others, factor 1 traits indicating manipulativeness, superficial charm, and pathological lying (see Hare et al., 2000), may likely bias malevolent creativity self-reports.

text.text: In support of these arguments, when linking the dark triad/tetrad to malevolent creativity in performance tests, robust associations like with malevolent creativity self-report are nowhere to be found.

As highlighted by a meta-analysis of Lebuda et al. (2021), links of narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy with performance on general, non-malevolent creativity tests are virtually zero (highest r = 0.06 for narcissism), suggesting that the dark triad and creative performance are mostly independent characteristics.

text.text: Findings for malevolent creativity performance (e.g., other-rated originality of ideas in a test) are similar.

In Perchtold-Stefan et al. (2024a), psychopathy was uncorrelated with creativity metrics on a malevolent creativity test (highest r = 0.05), although it showed large positive correlations with self-reports on the MCBS (r's ~ 0.50).
Likewise, Kapoor et al. (2025) found no significant associations between the dark tetrad and creativity of ideas in an unethical deception task (r's -0.04 for narcissism to 0.05 for sadism).

text.text: In Kapoor et al. (2026), participants higher on the dark tetrad also did not generate more creative deception ideas in situations where the explicit goal was to damage others. (r's -0.04 to 0.01).

text.text: Consequently, there is a question mark around the suitability of selfreport creativity measures, in particular for populations exhibiting elevated levels of the dark triad/tetrad.
Second, as arguably the bigger caveat, results with the MCBS itself as a self-report measure of malevolent creativity may stand on particularly shaky ground.

As recently summarized by Cropley (2026), the MCBS questionnaire itself seems to have poor validity, as it likely does not measure malevolent creativity, but rather, nonoriginal, malevolent tendencies (for similar arguments that the MCBS fails to capture originality, and may also conflate negative and malevolent creativity, see Reiter-Palmon, 2018; Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2025).

text.text: Overall, we thus consider evidence of dark triad/tetrad links to malevolent creativity performance weak at best.

However, before dismissing previous positive findings, this paper seeks further evidence to support the view that the dark triad/tetrad may in fact be a poor predictor of malevolent creativity if measured as individuals' capacity for malevolent creative idea generation.

Due to heavy reliance on malevolent creativity self-report, literature to date may have overemphasized the role of the dark triad/tetrad when it comes to individuals' capacity to generate creative and harmful ideas.
This may suggest that we have possibly been looking in the wrong place when trying to map (dark) personality aspects of malevolent creativity.
For this reason, in this paper, we aim to shed light on the matter by scrutinizing links between the dark triad/tetrad and malevolent creativity performance.
Data was collected in two independent studies previously conducted for larger research projects on individual differences in malevolent creativity (see methods).

Study 1 (n = 307) assessed dark triad personality traits, along with participants' capacity for malevolent creativity in a psychometric test for creative revenge ideation (MCT; 4-item version, Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2021a).

text.text: Study 2 (n = 287) assessed dark tetrad personality traits as well as malevolent creativity in a 2-item version of the MCT.

As a first step, Pearson's correlations were computed to obtain basic associations of the dark triad/tetrad with different indices of malevolent creativity performance (ideational fluency, malevolence of ideas, originality of ideas, total malevolent creativity; see Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2021ab, 2022ab, 2023 , 2024 , 2026).

text.text: As a second step, we ran multiple regression models to determine if certain aspects of the dark triad/tetrad, as well as their respective interactions, would predict malevolent creativity performance under control of demographics.
The present studies were not pre-registered.
Thus, we did not have specific a-priori hypotheses regarding associations of the dark triad/tetrad and malevolent creativity.

Yet, our more general expectation was that while individuals higher in these personality traits may generate more harmful ideas in malevolent creativity tasks, they may not generate more original ideas, and thus, not show higher malevolent creativity as per its definition (see Harris & Reiter-Palmon, 2015).

text.text: As malevolent creativity research extensively focused on the dark triad/tetrad in recent years, our two studies are intended to inform current and future discussions on the relevance of dark personality for dark creativity.

text.text: On the malevolent creativity test (MCT) by Perchtold-Stefan et al. (2021ab, 2022ab, 2023 , 2024 , 2026), participants generate creative ideas for taking revenge on unfair peers or associates.

text.text: In this test version, participants were instructed to generate harmful creative ideas to resolve four negative social scenarios, which include 1) a careless colleague spilling coffee on an expensive book, 2) a broken promise for money for helping out a neighbor, 3) competing with an unfair rival for a job interview, and 4) an inconsiderate roommate throwing a party during a busy work week.
Participants had three minutes to generate ideas for each item, which were written down in a sheet in from of them.

Following the standard coding procedure for the MCT, ideas were coded for fluency (number of non-identical ideas conforming to revenge instructions, i.e., reflecting at least minimal harm), malevolence (degree of harmfulness;1 = slightly malevolent to6 = highly malevolent), and originality (1 = very unoriginal to6 = very original).
One experienced rater determined fluency of ideas, three raters coded ideas for malevolence and originality.
Intra-class correlations (two-way random, consistency) for malevolence were ICC = .99, and for originality, were ICC = .94.

A total score of malevolent creativity was computed by summing up the number of malevolent ideas that were at least moderately original (≥3), conforming to the idea that malevolent creative ideas need to be both, harmful and original (see Harris & Reiter-Palmon, 2015).

Second, a main, step-wise multiple regression model was run to test links between the dark triad and total malevolent creativity.
At step 1, gender, age, and education were entered as demographical predictors.
At step 2, the dark triad traits narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy were entered.
At step 3, two-way interactions among the dark triad were entered.
Step 4 entered the three-way interaction of dark triad traits.
Followup models were computed for MCT malevolence, originality, and fluency.

Significant interaction effects were followed-up with the Jamovi package GAMLj (Galluci, 2019) to test simple effects of interactions with 5000 bootstraps, and to illustrate interaction effects across different levels of the moderator(s).

Statistical assumptions for the multiple regression models (i.e., ratio of cases to independent variables, normality, independence of errors, homoscedasticity, linearity, and absence of multicollinearity) were met.
A significance level of p < .05 (two-tailed) was applied for all analyses.

text.text: Neither the dark triad by itself nor their interactions showed any significant associations with total malevolent creativity in a performance test.

The strongest associations between the dark triad and malevolent creativity that were however, still weak in general terms, were observed for Machiavellianism and malevolence and originality of generated ideas (r's = 0.10).
Critically however, these miniscule associations failed to be significant both in correlations and multiple regression models controlling for demographics and other dark triad traits.
Accordingly, we find no evidence that individuals high in dark triad traits are more capable of generating creative ideas for harming others.

All participants signed informed content to participate in the study, which was approved by the authorized ethics committee.

text.text: Each trait is rated on seven items, on a scale from1 = strongly disagree to5 = strongly agree.
Malevolent creativity was measured with two items of the Malevolent Creativity Test (MCT).

The following situations were used: 1) a careless colleague spilling coffee over your expensive book and blaming you for it, and 2) a neighbor promising you money for help in renovating their apartment but later denying ever having such an agreement.
The situations were presented via LimeSurvey with digital vignettes, with a 3-minute time limit for idea generation per situation.
Participants typed their answers into a text box, with the survey automatically moving to the next items once the time was up.

In line with the previous study and the standard MCT scoring protocol, ideas were rated for ideational fluency (number of on-identical ideas that conform to malevolence instructions), malevolence (harmfulness of the ideas;1 = slightly malevolent to6 = highly malevolent) and originality of the ideas (1 = very unoriginal to6 = very original).

Malevolence and originality were rated by two independent and experienced raters, with good to excellent interrater agreement (ICC two-way mixed, consistency for malevolence = .84, for originality = .92).
As a final score, total malevolent creativity was calculated as the number of ideas that are at least moderately original (originality ≥ 3).

text.text: Applying the same analyses as study 1, first, Pearsons' correlations between all variables were computed.
Second, a main, step-wise multiple regression model was run to test links between the dark tetrad and total malevolent creativity.
At step 1, gender, age, and education were entered as demographical predictors.
At step 2, the dark tetrad traits narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism were entered.
At step 3, two-way interactions among the dark tetrad were entered.
Step 4 entered the three-way interactions, with Step 5 entering the four-way interaction.
Follow-up models were computed for MCT malevolence, originality, and fluency.

Significant interaction effects were followed-up with the Jamovi package GAMLj (Galluci, 2019) to test simple effects of interactions with 5000 bootstraps, and to illustrate interaction effects across different levels of the moderator(s).

Statistical assumptions for the multiple regression models (i.e., ratio of cases to independent variables, normality, independence of errors, homoscedasticity, linearity, and absence of multicollinearity) were met.
A significance level of p < .05 (two-tailed) was applied for all analyses.

text.text: Mirroring study 1, Machiavellianism and psychopathy showed weak positive correlations with MCT malevolence.
As the strongest, yet non-significant correlation with MCT creativity metrics, sadism showed a positive link to MCT originality (r = 0.11).
Additionally, narcissism weakly positively correlated with MCT fluency, but this link vanished in multiple regression models.

Yet, in these models, a significant three-way interaction of sadism x psychopathy x Machiavellianism emerged, showing that malevolent creativity was higher in individuals who reported a combination of higher sadism, higher Machiavellianism, and higher psychopathy.
Critically, this effect was small with f² = 0.02.

Other dark tetrad interaction effects emerged for MCT malevolence, originality, and fluency, mainly including links of higher sadism with higher MCT scores, combined with lower expressions of Machiavellianism and psychopathy.
However overall, these patterns for MCT subscales were rather inconsistent, and no effect exceeded f² = 0.02.

The goal of the present study was to review and extend evidence on previously reported associations of the dark triad/tetrad and malevolent creativity, following the idea that the relevance of the dark tetrad for malevolent creativity may have been overstated.

In two independent studies, we tested whether individuals higher in narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, or sadism exhibited a higher capacity for generating malevolent creative ideas in a performance test, as has often been inferred from large correlations of these dark traits with self-reported malevolent creativity (see Gao et al., 2022; Geng et al., 2024; Jia et al., 2020; Silva et al., 2025; Szabó et al., 2022).

text.text: Although study 1 examined the dark triad, and study 2 the dark tetrad, for brevity reasons, we will subsequently discuss our findings referring to the dark tetrad.
In both our studies, neither aspect of the dark tetrad displayed correlations larger than r = .10 with our composite metric of total malevolent creativity, and no correlation reached significance.

As the number of harmful revenge ideas also rated as original, total malevolent creativity reflects malevolent divergent thinking, i.e., coming up with a large pool of harmful original ideas, which research argues, maximizes chances of creatively hurting others in versatile ways (Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2021ab, 2022ab).
text.formatted: As the number of harmful revenge ideas also rated as original, total malevolent creativity reflects malevolent divergent thinking, i.e., coming up with a large pool of harmful original ideas, which research argues, maximizes chances of creatively hurting others in versatile ways <ref type="bibr">(Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2021ab, 2022ab)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, we find no evidence that higher scores on either aspect of the dark tetrad alone relate to a higher potential for overall malevolent creativity when prompted to come up with creative revenge ideas for unfair social situations.
Here, one may question the focus on generating many original ideas for harm, as in real-life, people may become deeply invested in elaborating and refining one highly harmful and original idea.
However, dark tetrad correlations with other-rated originality of ideas were equally non-significant.
Here, the largest correlation emerged for sadism and originality of ideas (r = .11), with this effect turning partially significant in multiple regression models.

Overall, our nonsignificant and negligible associations of narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism with creativity in harmful idea generation challenge the status quo of malevolent creativity research.
In the following, we discuss this from three different perspectives that may be useful for future investigations on the matter.

Explanation 1: There simply is no direct link of single dark tetrad aspects with malevolent creativity Given our findings, we need to consider that individuals scoring higher on single aspects of the dark tetrad do in fact not have a meaningfully higher capacity for malevolent creativity, although given their malevolent nature, we may have been led to believe that they do.

Previously, it has been argued that higher sadism may be especially relevant for malevolent creativity, as sadism is defined by enjoyment of suffering of others, despite lack of a personal relationship or contempt for the victim (e.g., Dow, 2023; Buckels et al., 2013).

text.text: As underlined by high correlations with bullying, malicious pranks, or online harassment of strangers (Ward, 2025), individuals higher in sadism delight in causing anybody harm.

text.text: This, as proposed by Dow (2023), they may achieve this through surprising and original means that catch others off guard, e.g., in the online world, by cyberstalking, doxing, catfishing, trolling, and generally terrorizing others for personal pleasure.

text.text: However, as we will discuss below, the degree of sadism relevant for such behaviors may be rather different that was is measured within a normal range of dark tetrad questionnaires applied in normal populations.

In support, in our malevolent creativity test, links of sadism and originality of ideas on our malevolent creativity test were trivial (r = 0.11), and more closely aligned with previous null findings for originality in deception tasks (Kapoor et al., 2025 (Kapoor et al., , 2026) ) than with presumably inflated correlations with malevolent creativity self-report (up to r = 0.72, Wang et al., 2026).

text.text: In sum, although we obtained partially significant associations of sadism with originality of ideas in multiple regression models, given the size of the effect (f² = 0.02), it is in doubt whether elevated sadism in nonclinical samples is truly meaningful in describing, and predicting, individuals' potential for creative harm.

Still, our regression models also allowed to test whether interactions of dark tetrad, i.e., higher expressions on multiple traits may be more relevant for malevolent creativity than higher scores on single traits.

In study 1, no significant interactions of the dark triad on malevolent creativity emerged, indicating that not even a combination of higher narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy explained variance in malevolent creativity.

However, in study 2, sadism changed this pattern, as threeway interactions of Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism predicted total malevolent creativity, as well as originality and malevolence of ideas.
The three-way interaction of higher expressions on all traits on total malevolent creativity presented the strongest effect that was however, still small in effect size terms (β = 0.27, f² = 0.02).

Interpreted together with correlational results for sadism, this suggests that higher instrumental thinking and strategic manipulation of others (Machiavellianism) as well as higher callousness, impulsivity, and lack of remorse (psychopathy) may not matter much for malevolent creativity by themselves.

Machiavellianism may not directly correlate with malevolent creativity, presumably because (negative) relationships are managed in very careful, strategic ways, depending on risks and gains of a situation (see Paulhus, 2014).

text.text: Similarly, individuals higher in psychopathy may show a stronger propensity for direct, and thus, effective aggression (Paulhus et al., 2018), with no perceived added value of creativity.

text.text: In fact, we may argue that if individuals only present elevated levels of (subclinical) psychopathy, they may care less for deception, trickery, and covering their tracks, and for this reason, show lower creativity.
This is also underlined by negative links of psychopathy to originality in our multiple regression models.

Yet, if higher sadism, and thus, the appetitive motivation to harm others for enjoyment, is added to the mix, strategic manipulation of Machiavellianism and callous impulsivity of psychopathy may contribute small, but meaningful ingredients for total malevolent creativity.

In general, our results are compatible with research findings that individuals with combinations of elevated dark triad/tetrad traits show more risky, deviant, and antisocial behaviors (Chabrol et al., 2015; Maheux-Caron et al., 2024; Nguyen et al., 2020).

text.text: As such, when it comes to dark personality, malevolent creativity may be best understood as emerging from an intricate constellation of antagonistic, impulsive, and manipulative traits.
This may explain why previous studies have obtained significant associations of composite antisocial personality measures with individuals' capacity for malevolent creativity in tests.

For example, Perchtold-Stefan et al. (2021a) reported that the DSM-5 maladaptive personality domain antagonism, encompassing grandiosity, manipulativeness, and deceitfulness, uniquely and positively predicted total malevolent creativity (also see Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2023).

text.text: Similarly, a combination of higher trait aggression and higher impulsivity has also been linked to higher malevolent creativity performance in other studies (Harris & Reiter-Palmon, 2015).

text.text: Still, in case of our "triple negative" dark tetrad interaction of Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism on malevolent creativity, the practical relevance of this effect must be questioned, which leads us to explanation 2.
As another perspective on our modest findings, research may have also rather persistently looked at the "wrong" people when scrutinizing dark tetrad links to malevolent creativity (Cropley, 2025).
text.formatted: As another perspective on our modest findings, research may have also rather persistently looked at the "wrong" people when scrutinizing dark tetrad links to malevolent creativity <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cropley, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: As such, the vast majority of malevolent creativity studies have been conducted in student populations that naturally, mostly show subclinical expressions of dark tetrad traits.
However, these are often discussed as if they met clinical thresholds for aversive cognitions and behaviors, including devastating malevolent creativity.
Yet, when looking at mean and maximum scores of malevolence on administered malevolent creativity tests or items, it seems that most tested individuals only generate ideas of moderate malevolence.
For example, in our study 1, only ~ 17 percent of participants presented average malevolence ratings higher than 3 (out of 6), while for study 2, it was only ~ 3 percent.
Importantly, this is no exception when looking at metrics of previous studies (see Batey et al., 2022; Kapoor et al., 2025 Kapoor et al., , 2026;; Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Importantly, this is no exception when looking at metrics of previous studies (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Batey et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Kapoor et al., 2025</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Kapoor et al., , 2026;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Together with often similarly modest scores for originality, we should thus consider that a large portion of tested individuals are simply not malevolent or creative enough, and thus, too "normal" to expect strong links of antisocial personality with malevolent creativity.

This is also corroborated by studies showing that the base-rate of an aversive personality constellation like elevated Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism, as reflected in our three-way interaction on malevolent creativity, is likely low.
Running latent profile analyses on personality in the workplace, She et al. (2025) found that 16% of their sample scored high on all aspects of the dark triad.

text.text: By comparison, in a community sample from Gómez-Leal et al. (2024), only seven percent scored high on all aspects of the dark tetrad.

text.text: While these percentages only serve as rough estimates regarding the prevalence of elevated dark tetrad traits, for our argument, they underline that individuals high in Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism only represent a minor portion of the general population.
Naturally, low prevalence does not imply low relevance.

Still, the idea that a small subgroup of individuals account for a substantial amount of creative harm in daily life is also rebuffed by research on emotional and social factors in malevolent creativity.

A variety of studies find that malevolent creativity can be elicited by negative emotions, conflict, threat, or negative environments in general, irrespective of antisocial personality traits (see Baas et al. 2019; Fousiani et al., 2025; Gutworth et al., 2018; Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2024b).

text.text: Additionally, it can be argued that the prevalence of malevolent creativity in daily life (lies, bullying, defamation, theft, pranks, sabotage, assault) is much higher than the range of action of a few severely antisocial personality profiles.

In sum, a configuration of high Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism may well be informative for understanding certain individuals' capacity for malevolent creativity, particularly when it comes to more extreme instances of harm, terrorism, warfare, or crime (see Hunter et al., 2022).

text.text: However, our findings (and their effect sizes) suggest that the relevance of subclinical dark tetrad expressions specifically may have been overemphasized by malevolent creativity research conducted in student and general population samples.

As one outline for future studies, it may be time to investigate dark personality -malevolent creativity links in populations more relevant to the matter: individuals who are either highly creative, or individuals who are capable of truly harmful actions towards others, or ideally, both.

Finally, we argue that previous research's overemphasis of the dark tetrad for malevolent creativity is likely due to misinterpretations of associations found for malevolent creativity self-report, and partially, misinterpretations of single indices in malevolent creativity tests, like malevolence of ideas.

Regarding the former, findings with the frequently used MCBS are now increasingly challenged, due to the questionnaires' negligible correlations with indicators of creativity (e.g., openness, creative selfefficacy, see Cropley, 2026).

text.text: However crucially, as noted by Hunter et al. (2022), neither deception, nor deviance, or crime and law breaking are malevolent creativity, if they are not creative (for similar arguments on aggression, see Harris & Reiter-Palmon, 2015).

text.text: In this respect, links of the dark tetrad and the MCBS may likely just be malevolence measures correlating with each other, and it should be considered that both have little to do with creativity.

Corroborating this idea, when more substantial correlations of the dark tetrad with malevolent creativity on performance tests emerged, they only did so for other-rated malevolence, i.e., antisocial individuals generating ideas that are more harmful (see Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2024a; Kapoor et al., 2025 Kapoor et al., , 2026)).

text.text: This is also reflected in our studies, where the largest effect was observed for links of sadism and malevolence of ideas in study 2 (r = 0.20).

Accordingly, it may be the case that individuals higher in the dark tetrad self-report more malevolent ideation, and also generate more harmful ideas on malevolent creativity tasks, but still lack the originality required for malevolent creativity.
Overall, in light of these arguments and our own findings, if the subclinical dark tetrad signals malevolent creativity, it appears to be so little that it may be irrelevant.
This calls for the development of better self-report scales for malevolent creativity behavior, and in general, more refined batteries for malevolent idea generation.
In both our studies, our samples were similar in age, gender composition (more women than men), and were highly educated.
Both studies also featured the same malevolent creativity task, with identical instructions, timings, and rating of ideas.
Still, as a limitation, in study 1, the MCT was administered in person, while in study 2, it was administered via an online survey, which may complicate comparisons.
As another limitations, our findings are based on specific, short scales of the dark triad and tetrad.
As such, our ideas and results should be further scrutinized with more extensive measures.
Still, previous research on malevolent creativity and dark personality also seems to have largely relied on short scales (see Table 1).

text.text: It is also possible that single aspects of the dark tetrad are more meaningfully linked to malevolent creativity if test scenarios more closely reflect particularities of the respective trait.

For example, narcissism may result in higher originality of ideas if test situations threaten ego, status, or resources (see Jones & Paulhus, 2010), while sadism may be more strongly related to unprovoked malevolent creativity, i.e., aggressing against unsuspecting weaker targets, even at a personal cost (Buckels et al., 2013).

text.text: Finally, our discussions only pertain to individuals' capacity for malevolent idea generation (potential) and cannot infer if certain dark tetrad traits would also lead to higher malevolent innovation.

While it also seems intuitive that individuals scoring higher in these traits would also more likely implement malevolent creative ideas in real-life (see Wang et al., 2025, for findings with the Malevolent Innovative Behavior Scale), future malevolent creativity tests should be expanded with idea rating protocols to determine the role of the dark tetrad in idea selection, and intended implementation (see Perchtold-Stefan et al., 2025).

text.text: In two independent studies, we find little evidence that the dark tetrad is meaningfully linked to a higher capacity for malevolent creativity.

While study 1 yielded null findings, in study 2, a (presumably very rare) combination of higher Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism predicted total malevolent creativity in multiple regression models.
Crucially however, no observed creativity effects exceeded f² = 0.02.

These associations appear trivial, especially in light of the huge emphasis placed on the dark tetrad by past malevolent creativity research, and the obtained, often large correlations of dark tetrad traits and malevolent creativity self-report.

From our perspective, it thus seems scholars may have overemphasized the relevance of the dark tetrad for malevolent idea generation in the general population, possibly at the expense of other, more relevant personality traits.

Importantly, our argument is not that antisocial personality is irrelevant for understanding everyday manifestations of malevolent creativity, but that the dark tetrad specifically may be less important than previously assumed.
When it comes to explaining the tremendous variety and perilousness of malevolent creativity in daily-life, perhaps it is time to move on to other darker shores.
